unit_label: Module B unit 3 annexure: capital elements, credit conversion, counterparty risk, collateral and RWA

facts.statement: Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital of an Indian bank comprises common shares meeting the regulatory criteria, stock surplus (share premium) from common shares, statutory reserves, capital reserves from sale proceeds of assets, the AFS reserve (any negative balance is deducted), revaluation reserves of property at a discount of 55 per cent (if the bank can sell the property readily, the reserve is shown in Schedule 2 of the balance sheet, valuations are realistic and taken from two independent valuers at least every three years, the auditors have not qualified the revaluation, and the valuation instructions are followed; revaluation reserves that do not qualify for CET1 do not qualify for Tier 2), foreign currency translation reserve at a discount of 25 per cent (shown in Schedule 2 and not qualified by the auditors), other disclosed free reserves, the balance in the profit and loss account at the end of the previous year, current year profits on a quarterly basis if the statements are audited or limited-reviewed (eligible profit EPt = NPt − 0.25 × D × t, where D is the average dividend paid in the last three years and t runs from 1 to 4), and minority interest in common shares of consolidated subsidiaries, less regulatory adjustments. Minority interest is recognised only where it is considered to be available to absorb losses at the group level: common shares of a consolidated subsidiary that is itself a bank qualify, while minority interest in non-bank subsidiaries is not included in the group's CET1. For foreign bank branches CET1 consists of interest-free head office funds kept for capital norms, statutory reserves, remittable surplus retained in India, interest-free funds for property acquisition, capital reserve from asset sales, and the same revaluation and translation reserve treatment. The courseware (printed pp. 364-367) does not mention the AFS reserve and states the quarterly profit condition as provisions not deviating by more than 25 per cent from the average of the four quarters; the Directions are taught.
facts.locator: Directions paragraphs 12 and 27; S03 printed pp. 364-367

facts.statement: Additional Tier 1 capital of an Indian bank consists of perpetual non-cumulative preference shares (PNCPS) meeting the requirements, stock surplus from those instruments, debt capital instruments (perpetual debt instruments) eligible for Additional Tier 1, any other instrument notified by the Reserve Bank, and Additional Tier 1 instruments issued by consolidated subsidiaries and held by third parties that meet the criteria, less regulatory adjustments. For a foreign bank's branches it consists of head office borrowings in foreign currency that meet the requirements, any other item allowed by the Reserve Bank, less adjustments. Tier 2 capital has a single set of criteria for debt instruments and consists of general provisions and loss reserves (general provisions on standard assets, floating provisions, incremental provisions for unhedged foreign currency exposures, provisions for country exposures, the investment reserve account, excess provisions from the sale of NPAs and the countercyclical provisioning buffer, together admitted up to a maximum of 1.25 per cent of total credit risk-weighted assets under the standardised approach; provisions ascribed to identified deterioration of particular assets, such as specific provisions on NPAs, are excluded), debt capital instruments, preference share capital instruments (PCPS, RNCPS, RCPS), stock surplus from those, Tier 2 instruments of consolidated subsidiaries held by third parties that meet the criteria, revaluation reserves at a discount of 55 per cent and other instruments notified by the Reserve Bank, less regulatory adjustments. The courseware states an additional cap of 0.6 per cent of credit risk-weighted assets under the internal ratings based approach, which does not apply to banks using the standardised approach; its transitional note (recognition of instruments that no longer qualify capped at 90 per cent from 1 January 2013, reducing by 10 percentage points a year) is historical.
facts.locator: Directions Chapter III, B and C (Tier 2 provisions paragraph); S03 printed pp. 365-368

facts.statement: Regulatory adjustments (deductions) apply at solo and consolidated level and cover: goodwill and all other intangible assets (deducted from CET1, net of any associated deferred tax liability that would be extinguished); deferred tax assets (those from accumulated losses are deducted in full; those from timing differences may instead be recognised in CET1 up to 10 per cent of CET1 at the bank's discretion after the other adjustments); the cash flow hedge reserve; the shortfall of the stock of provisions to expected losses; gains on sale related to securitisation transactions; cumulative gains and losses due to changes in own credit risk on fair-valued financial liabilities; defined benefit pension fund assets and liabilities; investments in own shares (treasury stock); investments in the capital of banking, financial and insurance entities; equity investments in non-financial subsidiaries; and intra-group transactions and exposures. Goodwill included in the valuation of a significant investment outside regulatory consolidation is also deducted, and losses of the current and earlier periods are deducted from CET1 if not already deducted.

Non-market-related off-balance sheet items are converted to credit equivalents by multiplying the contracted amount by a credit conversion factor (CCF): 100 per cent for direct credit substitutes (general guarantees of indebtedness, standby letters of credit serving as financial guarantees for loans and securities, credit enhancements, liquidity facilities for securitisation) and acceptances, for sale and repurchase agreements and asset sales with recourse where credit risk remains with the bank, for forward asset purchases, forward deposits and partly paid shares and securities, for lending of banks' securities or posting securities as collateral, for commitments with certain drawdown and for unconditional take-out finance; 50 per cent for certain transaction-related contingent items (performance bonds, bid bonds, warranties, indemnities and standby letters of credit related to a particular transaction), for note issuance and revolving underwriting facilities, for other commitments with original maturity over one year and for conditional take-out finance; 20 per cent for short-term self-liquidating trade letters of credit (documentary credits collateralised by the shipment) and for other commitments with original maturity up to one year; and 0 per cent for commitments that are unconditionally cancellable at any time without notice (subject to the bank showing it can actually cancel; for borrowers with aggregate fund-based working capital limits of ₹150 crore or more from the banking system, the undrawn portion of cash credit and overdraft limits attracts 20 per cent regardless). The undrawn portion of a fund-based facility is the maximum unused portion that could be drawn during the remaining period; for a staged term loan the undrawn portion is measured with reference to the stage for which the bank's approval has been given. An irrevocable commitment to provide an off-balance sheet facility takes the lower of the two applicable CCFs. The courseware table (printed pp. 368-369 and 388) agrees.
facts.locator: Directions paragraphs 83 and 84 and Table 15; S03 printed pp. 368-369, 379 and 388

facts.statement: Counterparty credit risk (CCR) is the risk that the counterparty to a transaction could default before the final settlement of its cash flows; it is bilateral, because the market value of the transaction can be positive or negative for either party. It arises in over-the-counter derivatives, exchange traded derivatives and securities financing transactions (repos, reverse repos, securities lending and borrowing, margin lending), whose value depends on market valuation and which may be subject to netting, collateral and remargining. The capital charge covers default risk and credit migration risk reflected in credit value adjustment (CVA), the adjustment to the mid-market value of a portfolio of trades for the credit risk of the counterparty. A central counterparty (CCP) interposes itself between counterparties, becoming the buyer to every seller and seller to every buyer; a qualifying CCP is licensed and supervised as such in line with the CPSS-IOSCO principles. A clearing member is a member or direct participant of a CCP; a client transacts through a clearing member. Initial margin is funded collateral posted to mitigate the CCP's potential future exposure; variation margin is collateral posted daily or intraday on price movements; default funds are mutualised loss-sharing contributions. Current exposure is the larger of zero and the market value that would be lost on default. For OTC derivatives the Directions use the Current Exposure Method: the credit equivalent is current credit exposure (the sum of positive mark-to-market values) plus potential future credit exposure (notional principal multiplied by an add-on factor for the instrument and residual maturity, whatever the mark-to-market). Under the Directions as substituted from 10 March 2026 the add-on factors are, for interest rate contracts, 0.25 per cent up to one year, 0.50 per cent over one to five years and 1.50 per cent over five years, and, for exchange rate contracts and gold, 1.00, 5.00 and 7.50 per cent; the courseware table (0.5, 1, 3 and 2, 10, 15 per cent) is older and not taught. With legally effective bilateral netting the add-on is ANet = 0.4 × AGross + 0.6 × NGR × AGross, where NGR is net replacement cost over gross replacement cost. No add-on is calculated for single currency floating/floating swaps.
facts.locator: Directions paragraph 85 and Table 16; S03 printed pp. 369-372

facts.statement: The Directions allow banks to use ratings of seven domestic agencies, in alphabetical order Acuite, Brickwork, CARE, CRISIL, ICRA, India Ratings and INFOMERICS (the courseware lists six, including SMERA, which is now Acuite), and of international agencies Fitch, Moody's and Standard and Poor's (and CareEdge Global IFSC for non-resident corporates). Long-term ratings map to standardised approach risk weights of 20 per cent for AAA, 30 per cent for AA, 50 per cent for A, 100 per cent for BBB and 150 per cent for BB and below, with a plus or minus notation taking the main category; an unrated claim gets 100 per cent, rising to 150 per cent where the aggregate exposure from the banking system exceeds ₹200 crore (or exceeds ₹100 crore for exposures rated earlier and now unrated). Short-term ratings are issue-specific and map A1+ to 20 per cent, A1 to 30 per cent, A2 to 50 per cent, A3 to 100 per cent and A4 and D to 150 per cent. Only solicited ratings may be used. With one rating it is used; with two ratings mapping to different risk weights the higher risk weight applies; with three or more the two lowest risk weights are considered and the higher of those applies. A long-term rating warranting 150 per cent makes all unrated claims on the same counterparty 150 per cent, unless risk mitigation applies.
facts.locator: Directions paragraphs 131 to 151, Tables 25 and 26; S03 printed pp. 372-373

facts.statement: In the comprehensive approach, eligible financial collateral comprises cash and fixed deposit receipts or certificates of deposit issued by the lending bank and held with it; gold including jewellery converted to 99.99 purity; securities issued by the Central and State Governments; Kisan Vikas Patra and National Savings Certificates if there is no lock-in and they can be encashed within the holding period; life insurance policies with a declared surrender value from a regulated insurer; debt securities rated at least BBB minus (or A3 for short-term) by a chosen agency when issued by public sector entities and others, with sufficient market liquidity; certain unrated senior debt of a bank listed on a recognised exchange; and units of mutual funds with a publicly quoted daily NAV that invest only in eligible instruments. Re-securitisations are not eligible whatever their rating. The exposure after mitigation is E* = max{0, [E × (1 + He) − C × (1 − Hc − Hfx)]}, where He and Hc are the haircuts for the exposure and the collateral and Hfx is the currency mismatch haircut; E* is multiplied by the counterparty risk weight. Banks in India use only the standard supervisory haircuts (assuming daily mark-to-market, daily remargining and a ten business day holding period). The currency mismatch haircut is 8 per cent. Table 27 haircuts: Government of India and State Government securities 0.5, 2 and 4 per cent for residual maturity up to one year, over one to five years and over five years; other domestic debt rated AAA to AA or A1 1, 4 and 8 per cent, rated A to BBB or A2 and A3 and eligible unrated bank securities 2, 6 and 12 per cent; cash in the same currency 0; gold 15 per cent; securitisation exposures rated AAA to AA 2, 8 and 16 per cent and A to BBB 4, 12 and 24 per cent (the courseware gives 13 for the last cell, which differs from the Directions); units of mutual funds take the highest haircut applicable to the securities in which they may invest. A zero haircut may be applied to National Savings Certificates, Kisan Vikas Patras, surrender value of insurance policies and the bank's own deposits. Where the exposure is unrated or the bank lends non-eligible instruments the exposure haircut is 25 per cent. A basket of collateral has a haircut equal to the weighted average of its components. The minimum holding period is five business days for repo-style transactions, ten for other capital market transactions and twenty for secured lending; haircuts are scaled by H = H10 × √[(NR + TM − 1) ÷ 10], where NR is the number of business days between remargining or revaluation and TM the minimum holding period. For maturity mismatch the collateral value is adjusted as Pa = P × (t − 0.25) ÷ (T − 0.25), where T is the lesser of five years and the residual maturity of the exposure and t the lesser of T and the residual maturity of the protection.
facts.locator: Directions paragraphs 157 to 165 and Tables 27 to 29; S03 printed pp. 373-377

facts.statement: The courseware describes credit risk-weighted assets under the standardised approach as a five-stage process: determine the adjusted exposure, determine the allowable reduction, determine the applicable risk weight, determine the risk-weighted asset for the exposure, and consolidate the RWAs of all exposures. The exposure on a borrower is the outstanding balance of fund-based facilities, plus the credit equivalent of the undrawn portion of fund-based facilities (20 per cent for limits other than term loans and for the term loan portion to be drawn within a year, 50 per cent for the term loan portion to be drawn after a year, nil where cancellable at any time without notice) and the credit equivalent of non-fund-based exposures (outstanding multiplied by the CCF). Allowable reduction arises from deposits under lien (allowable reduction = C × [1 − Hfx] × Mf, capped at the exposure, with Hfx 0.08 for a currency mismatch) and eligible financial collateral; the risk weight of the guarantor replaces the borrower's on the guaranteed part where the guarantor is a sovereign, bank, DICGC, CGTSI or ECGC or rated AA minus or better (the courseware gives 20 per cent for AAA and 30 per cent for AA guarantors), with adjusted guaranteed amount = G × (1 − Hfx) × Mf. RWA of an exposure is its net adjusted exposure times the risk weight. Capital charges for market risk and operational risk are multiplied by 12.5 to give risk-weighted assets, total RWA is the sum for credit, market and operational risk, Tier 1 CRAR is eligible Tier 1 capital divided by total RWA and total CRAR is eligible total capital divided by total RWA. The courseware's list of risk weights by exposure type is of earlier vintage and is not taught; the Directions' current risk weights are covered in the unit proper.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 378-388 (stages, exposure, reduction, guarantees, CRAR example); Directions paragraphs 83 to 84, 162

payload.title: Common Equity Tier 1 capital and minority interest
payload.core_explanation_md:
**CET1 (Indian banks)** = **common shares + share premium + statutory reserves + capital reserves (asset sales) + AFS reserve (negative balance deducted) + revaluation reserves (at a 55% discount) + FCTR (at a 25% discount)** **+ other free reserves + previous year's profit and loss balance + current profit (quarterly) + minority interest in common shares of banking subsidiaries − regulatory deductions**.

| Reserve | Counts | Conditions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Revaluation (property)** | **at a 55% discount** | **saleable freely; in Schedule 2; two independent valuers every 3 years; no audit qualification** |
| **FCTR** | **at a 25% discount** | **in Schedule 2; no audit qualification** |

**Current-year profit** counts **quarterly** if **audited or limited-reviewed**: **EPt = NPt − 0.25 × D × t** (**D** = average dividend in the last three years).

**Minority interest**: only where it will **absorb losses at group level** — **common shares of a bank subsidiary count; minority interest in non-bank subsidiaries does not**.

payload.title: Additional Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Tier | Main elements |
| --- | --- |
| **Additional Tier 1** | **perpetual non-cumulative preference shares (PNCPS)** and their **share premium**; **perpetual debt instruments**; **other instruments notified by RBI**; **AT1 of consolidated subsidiaries held by third parties**; **less deductions** |
| **Tier 2** | **general provisions and loss reserves** (**standard asset provisions, floating provisions, country exposure provisions, investment reserve account, countercyclical buffer**) **up to 1.25% of credit RWA**; **debt capital instruments**; **PCPS, RNCPS, RCPS**; **revaluation reserves at a 55% discount**; **less deductions** |

**Excluded from Tier 2**: **provisions for identified deterioration, such as specific provisions on NPAs**.

The courseware's **0.6% internal-ratings cap** is for banks using the internal ratings approach, **not for standardised-approach banks**.

payload.title: Regulatory deductions
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Deducted from capital (solo and consolidated)**

1. **Goodwill and other intangibles** (**net of related deferred tax liability**)
2. **Deferred tax assets**: **from accumulated losses: deducted in full**; **from timing differences: may be recognised up to 10% of CET1**
3. **Cash flow hedge reserve**
4. **Shortfall of the stock of provisions to expected losses**
5. **Gain on sale related to securitisation**
6. **Cumulative gains and losses from changes in own credit risk on fair-valued liabilities**
7. **Defined benefit pension fund assets and liabilities**
8. **Investments in own shares (treasury stock)**
9. **Investments in capital of banking, financial and insurance entities**
10. **Equity investments in non-financial subsidiaries**
11. **Intra-group transactions and exposures**

Current and brought-forward **losses** are also deducted from **CET1** if not already deducted.

payload.title: Credit conversion factors for non-market items
payload.core_explanation_md:
| CCF | Items |
| --- | --- |
| **100%** | **direct credit substitutes** (**general guarantees of indebtedness, financial standby LCs**), **acceptances**, **sale and repurchase / asset sales with recourse**, **forward asset purchases and partly paid shares**, **commitments with certain drawdown**, **lending or posting of securities as collateral**, **unconditional take-out finance** |
| **50%** | **performance and bid bonds, warranties, indemnities, transaction-related standby LCs**; **note issuance and revolving underwriting facilities**; **other commitments over one year**; **conditional take-out finance** |
| **20%** | **short-term self-liquidating trade LCs**; **other commitments up to one year** |
| **0%** | **commitments unconditionally cancellable at any time** (bank must be able to cancel) |

**Special rules**: **undrawn = maximum unused portion that could be drawn**; **borrowers with working capital limits of ₹150 crore or more: 20% on undrawn cash credit and overdraft limits even if cancellable**; **irrevocable commitments take the lower of two CCFs**.

**Credit equivalent = amount × CCF**; it is then **risk-weighted** like a loan.

payload.title: Counterparty credit risk terms and the current exposure method
payload.core_explanation_md:
**CCR** = **risk that the counterparty defaults before final settlement of cash flows**; **bilateral** (**value can be positive or negative for either side**); arises in **OTC derivatives, exchange-traded derivatives and securities financing transactions**.

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **CVA** | **adjustment to mid-market value for the counterparty's credit risk** |
| **CCP / QCCP** | **clearing house that becomes buyer to every seller**; **qualifying** = **licensed, supervised, CPSS-IOSCO consistent** |
| **Initial margin** | **collateral posted to cover the CCP's potential future exposure** |
| **Variation margin** | **collateral posted daily or intraday on price moves** |
| **Default fund** | **mutualised loss-sharing contribution** |
| **Current exposure** | **larger of zero and the market value that would be lost on default** |

**Current Exposure Method (OTC derivatives)**: **credit equivalent = current credit exposure (positive mark-to-market) + notional × add-on factor**.

| Add-on (Directions, from March 2026) | ≤ 1 year | 1–5 years | > 5 years |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Interest rate** | **0.25%** | **0.50%** | **1.50%** |
| **Exchange rate and gold** | **1.00%** | **5.00%** | **7.50%** |

**Netting**: **ANet = 0.4 × AGross + 0.6 × NGR × AGross**; **no add-on for single-currency floating/floating swaps**.

payload.title: External ratings and risk weights
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Agencies**: **domestic** — **Acuite, Brickwork, CARE, CRISIL, ICRA, India Ratings, INFOMERICS**; **international** — **Fitch, Moody's, S&P** (**CareEdge Global IFSC** for non-resident corporates). **Solicited ratings only**.

| Long-term rating | Risk weight | Short-term | Risk weight |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **AAA** | **20%** | **A1+** | **20%** |
| **AA** | **30%** | **A1** | **30%** |
| **A** | **50%** | **A2** | **50%** |
| **BBB** | **100%** | **A3** | **100%** |
| **BB and below** | **150%** | **A4 and D** | **150%** |
| **Unrated** | **100%** (**150%** if aggregate banking-system exposure **> ₹200 crore**) | | |

- **+ or −** takes the **main category**.
- **Multiple ratings**: **one rating: use it**; **two that differ: the higher risk weight**; **three or more: take the two lowest risk weights and use the higher**.
- A **150% long-term rating** makes **all unrated claims on that issuer 150%** (unless mitigated).

payload.title: Eligible collateral, haircuts and the E* formula
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Eligible financial collateral**: **cash and own bank deposits/FDRs; gold (99.99 purity); Central and State Government securities; KVP and NSC (no lock-in); insurance policies with surrender value; rated debt at least BBB− (A3 short-term) with market liquidity; certain unrated senior bank debt; mutual fund units with daily NAV**. **Re-securitisations: never eligible**.

**E* = max{0, E × (1 + He) − C × (1 − Hc − Hfx)}**, then **RWA = E* × risk weight**.

| Collateral (≤1 yr / 1–5 yrs / >5 yrs) | Haircut |
| --- | --- |
| **Government securities** | **0.5% / 2% / 4%** |
| **Domestic debt AAA to AA, A1** | **1% / 4% / 8%** |
| **Domestic debt A to BBB, A2, A3, eligible unrated bank debt** | **2% / 6% / 12%** |
| **Cash, same currency** | **0%** |
| **Gold** | **15%** |
| **Securitisation AAA to AA** | **2% / 8% / 16%** |
| **Securitisation A to BBB** | **4% / 12% / 24%** |

**Currency mismatch haircut: 8%**. **Unrated exposure or non-eligible instrument lent: 25%**. **Zero haircut**: **NSC, KVP, surrender value, own deposits**. **Standard supervisory haircuts only** are used in India.

**Holding period**: **repo-style 5 days; other capital market 10; secured lending 20** — **H = H10 × √[(NR + TM − 1) ÷ 10]**. **Maturity mismatch**: **Pa = P × (t − 0.25) ÷ (T − 0.25)**.

payload.title: From exposure to capital ratio: the five stages
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Five stages (courseware)**: **1 adjusted exposure → 2 allowable reduction → 3 applicable risk weight → 4 RWA of the exposure → 5 consolidation**.

**Adjusted exposure** = **funded outstanding + credit equivalent of undrawn fund-based limits + credit equivalent of non-fund-based items**.

**Allowable reduction**: **deposits under lien: C × (1 − Hfx) × Mf** (capped at the exposure; **Hfx 0.08 if currencies differ**); **financial collateral: via E***; **guarantees**: the **guarantor's risk weight replaces the borrower's on the guaranteed part** (adjusted amount **G × (1 − Hfx) × Mf**).

**Capital ratio**: **market and operational risk capital × 12.5 = RWA**; **Total RWA = credit + market + operational**; **Tier 1 ratio = Tier 1 ÷ total RWA**; **total ratio = total capital ÷ total RWA**.

The courseware's own **list of risk weights by exposure type** is older and **not taught here**.

payload.title: Credit equivalent of one borrower's facilities
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a borrower has a cash credit limit of ₹200 lakh with ₹120 lakh drawn, and a term loan with ₹100 lakh undrawn of which ₹40 lakh will be drawn within a year and ₹60 lakh after a year. It also has non-fund-based items: a financial guarantee of ₹90 lakh, a performance guarantee of ₹80 lakh and a documentary letter of credit of ₹40 lakh. Compute the credit equivalent of the undrawn and off-balance sheet items.

worked_steps.description: Credit equivalent of cash credit at 20%.
Term loan within a year at 20%.
Term loan after a year at 50%.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: The credit equivalent of the undrawn and off-balance sheet items is ₹192 lakh

self_check.prompt_text: Why does the financial guarantee carry 100% but the performance guarantee only 50%?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A financial guarantee is a direct credit substitute whose loss depends on the borrower's credit standing, while a performance guarantee is a transaction-related contingent item.

payload.title: The current exposure method for two derivatives
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a bank has an interest rate swap with a notional of ₹1,000 crore, residual maturity three years and a mark-to-market value of +₹6 crore, and a forward exchange contract with notional ₹500 crore, residual maturity eight months and mark-to-market value of −₹2 crore. Compute the total credit equivalent using the Directions' add-on factors.

worked_steps.description: Forward current exposure (negative value counts as zero).

payload.final_answer_with_unit: The total credit equivalent is ₹16 crore, to be multiplied by the counterparty risk weight

self_check.prompt_text: Why does the forward still carry an add-on although its value is negative?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The potential future exposure is based on the notional and applies whatever the current mark-to-market value, since the value may turn positive.

payload.title: Exposure after collateral, with and without currency mismatch
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a corporate loan of ₹100 lakh (no exposure haircut because loans are not marked to market) is secured by two alternative collaterals. Case A: A-rated domestic corporate debt securities of ₹30 lakh with residual maturity of 3 years, same currency. Case B: AAA domestic debt securities of ₹40 lakh with residual maturity of 6 years, held in a different currency. The borrower is BBB rated. Compute the exposure after mitigation and the risk-weighted asset in each case.

worked_steps.description: Case A haircut (A to BBB, 1–5 years).
Case B haircuts (AAA to AA over 5 years; currency mismatch).
Risk weight of a BBB borrower.
Risk-weighted assets, Case A and Case B.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: The risk-weighted assets are ₹71.80 lakh in Case A and ₹66.40 lakh in Case B

self_check.prompt_text: Why does the currency mismatch reduce the benefit of the collateral?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The collateral value is cut by an 8 per cent haircut for possible exchange rate moves, so less of the exposure is covered.

payload.title: Adjusting collateral for maturity mismatch
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: after haircuts, collateral is worth ₹60 lakh and has a residual maturity of 2 years, while the exposure of ₹100 lakh has a residual maturity of 4 years. Compute the maturity-adjusted collateral and the exposure after risk mitigation.

worked_steps.description: T is the lesser of 5 years and the exposure's residual maturity.
t is the lesser of T and the protection's residual maturity.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: The adjusted collateral is ₹28.00 lakh and the exposure after mitigation is ₹72.00 lakh

self_check.prompt_text: What would the adjusted collateral be if the collateral's residual maturity were also 4 years?
self_check.expected_takeaway: There would be no maturity mismatch, so the collateral would keep its full ₹60 lakh value.

payload.title: A capital adequacy ratio from components
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a bank has Tier 1 capital of ₹2,100 crore and Tier 2 capital of ₹900 crore. Its credit risk-weighted assets are ₹14,000 crore, the capital charge for market risk is ₹640 crore and the capital charge for operational risk is ₹360 crore. Compute the Tier 1 and total capital ratios and compare the total with the 11.5% minimum including the conservation buffer.
payload.final_answer_with_unit: Tier 1 ratio is 7.92% and the total capital ratio is 11.32%, below the 11.5% minimum with buffer

self_check.prompt_text: What capital would remove the gap, holding RWA constant?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 11.5% of ₹26,500 crore is about ₹3,047.5 crore, so roughly ₹47.5 crore more capital.

payload.stem_md: Which of the following is an element of Common Equity Tier 1 capital of an Indian bank?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Statutory reserves are a CET1 element; PNCPS are Additional Tier 1 and provisions and debt instruments are Tier 2.

payload.stem_md: At what discount may revaluation reserves arising from the revaluation of property be reckoned as CET1 capital?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Revaluation reserves count at a discount of 55 per cent, subject to the conditions.

payload.stem_md: At what discount may a bank reckon foreign currency translation reserve as CET1 capital?
payload.correct_explanation_md: The FCTR may be reckoned at a discount of 25 per cent.

payload.stem_md: Which of the following is an Additional Tier 1 capital instrument?

options.text_md: Revaluation reserves at 55 per cent discount

payload.correct_explanation_md: PNCPS and perpetual debt instruments that meet the requirements are Additional Tier 1.

payload.stem_md: General provisions on standard assets, floating provisions and similar items together are admitted as Tier 2 capital up to what maximum, for a bank using the standardised approach?

options.text_md: 1.25 per cent of total credit risk-weighted assets

payload.correct_explanation_md: These provisions are admitted up to a maximum of 1.25 per cent of total credit RWAs under the standardised approach.

payload.stem_md: Which of the following is deducted from CET1 capital?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Goodwill and all other intangible assets are deducted from CET1.

payload.stem_md: Deferred tax assets arising from timing differences (other than those related to accumulated losses) may, at the bank's discretion, be recognised in CET1 up to what limit?
payload.correct_explanation_md: DTAs relating to timing differences may be recognised up to 10 per cent of CET1 capital, after the other regulatory adjustments.

payload.stem_md: How is minority interest in a non-bank consolidated subsidiary treated in the group's CET1 capital?

options.text_md: It is included at a 55 per cent discount
It is included if the subsidiary is profitable

payload.correct_explanation_md: Minority interest in subsidiaries which are not banks is not included in the group's regulatory capital.

payload.stem_md: What credit conversion factor applies to direct credit substitutes such as general guarantees of indebtedness?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Direct credit substitutes carry a CCF of 100 per cent because the loss depends on the creditworthiness of the party.

payload.stem_md: What credit conversion factor applies to performance bonds and bid bonds?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Transaction-related contingent items such as performance bonds, bid bonds and warranties carry 50 per cent.

payload.stem_md: What credit conversion factor applies to short-term self-liquidating trade letters of credit collateralised by the underlying shipment?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Short-term self-liquidating trade letters of credit carry 20 per cent.

payload.stem_md: Commitments that the bank can cancel unconditionally at any time without notice attract which CCF, provided the bank can actually cancel them?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Unconditionally cancellable commitments carry 0 per cent, subject to the bank demonstrating that it can cancel.

payload.stem_md: A borrower has aggregate fund-based working capital limits of ₹150 crore or more from the banking system. What CCF applies to the undrawn portion of its cash credit and overdraft limits?

options.text_md: 20 per cent, whether or not cancellable

payload.correct_explanation_md: For such borrowers the undrawn portion of cash credit and overdraft limits attracts 20 per cent irrespective of cancellability.

payload.stem_md: Counterparty credit risk is best described as the risk that

options.text_md: Interest rates move against the bank
A loan is not repaid by a borrower in a unilateral exposure
The counterparty to a transaction could default before final settlement of its cash flows

payload.correct_explanation_md: CCR is the risk that the counterparty could default before final settlement; unlike a loan, exposure is bilateral.

payload.stem_md: What does a central counterparty do?

options.text_md: It lends to all clearing members
It becomes the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer

payload.correct_explanation_md: A CCP interposes itself between counterparties, ensuring the performance of open contracts.

payload.stem_md: Under the Current Exposure Method, the credit equivalent amount of an OTC derivative equals

options.text_md: The positive mark-to-market value plus notional multiplied by the add-on factor

payload.correct_explanation_md: It is the sum of current credit exposure and potential future credit exposure.

payload.stem_md: What risk weight applies under the standardised approach to a claim rated AA (long-term) by a chosen domestic agency?
payload.correct_explanation_md: AAA gets 20 per cent, AA 30 per cent, A 50 per cent and BBB 100 per cent.

payload.stem_md: If a bank has two ratings for a claim from chosen agencies that map to different risk weights, which risk weight applies?

options.text_md: The one from the older rating

payload.correct_explanation_md: With two ratings mapping into different risk weights, the higher risk weight is applied.

payload.stem_md: How many domestic credit rating agencies does the 2025 Capital Adequacy Directions allow banks to use?
payload.correct_explanation_md: The Directions list Acuite, Brickwork, CARE, CRISIL, ICRA, India Ratings and INFOMERICS.

payload.stem_md: An unrated corporate claim attracts what risk weight, when the aggregate exposure to the borrower from the banking system exceeds ₹200 crore?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Unrated claims get 100 per cent, rising to 150 per cent where aggregate banking-system exposure exceeds ₹200 crore.

payload.stem_md: Which of these is NOT eligible financial collateral?

options.text_md: Securities issued by the Central Government
Cash deposits with the lending bank

payload.correct_explanation_md: Re-securitisations are not eligible financial collateral irrespective of any credit ratings.

payload.stem_md: What is the standard supervisory haircut for a currency mismatch between exposure and collateral?
payload.correct_explanation_md: The standard supervisory haircut for currency risk is 8 per cent.

payload.stem_md: What standard supervisory haircut applies to gold accepted as collateral?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Gold carries a haircut of 15 per cent.

payload.stem_md: Which haircut approach must banks in India use for collateralised transactions?

options.text_md: Their own estimates of market price volatility

payload.correct_explanation_md: Banks in India use only the standard supervisory haircuts for both the exposure and the collateral.

payload.stem_md: In the courseware's five-stage process for credit risk-weighted assets, what is the first stage?
payload.correct_explanation_md: The stages are adjusted exposure, allowable reduction, applicable risk weight, RWA of the exposure and consolidation.

payload.stem_md: A cash credit limit of ₹250 lakh has ₹180 lakh drawn and is not unconditionally cancellable. What is the credit equivalent of the undrawn portion at a 20% CCF, in ₹ lakh?
An irrevocable commitment with an original maturity of 18 months has an undrawn portion of ₹200 lakh. What is the credit equivalent at the CCF for commitments over one year, in ₹ lakh?
A bank has issued bid bonds of ₹60 lakh and has an outstanding short-term documentary letter of credit of ₹100 lakh. What is the total credit equivalent, in ₹ lakh?
An interest rate swap has a notional of ₹800 crore and a residual maturity of 4 years. What is the potential future credit exposure under the Directions' add-on factors, in ₹ crore, to two decimals?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 2 decimal places.

payload.stem_md: A forward exchange contract has a notional of ₹300 crore, a residual maturity of 10 months and a positive mark-to-market value of ₹3 crore. What is its credit equivalent under the Current Exposure Method, in ₹ crore?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Add-on 1.00% × 300 = 3; credit equivalent = 3 + 3 = 6.

payload.stem_md: A loan of ₹100 lakh (no exposure haircut, same currency) is secured by A-rated domestic corporate debt of ₹35 lakh with a residual maturity of 7 years. What is the exposure after risk mitigation, in ₹ lakh, to two decimals?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 2 decimal places.

payload.stem_md: A loan of ₹80 lakh (no exposure haircut, same currency) is secured by gold collateral of ₹50 lakh. What is the exposure after risk mitigation, in ₹ lakh, to two decimals?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 2 decimal places.

payload.stem_md: A bank using the standardised approach has general provisions and other eligible items totalling ₹280 crore and total credit risk-weighted assets of ₹18,000 crore. How much can be admitted as Tier 2 capital from these items, in ₹ crore?

A repo-style transaction has a ten-day standard haircut of 4% for the collateral, daily remargining (NR = 1) and a minimum holding period of 5 business days. What is the adjusted haircut in per cent, to two decimals?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 2 decimal places.

unresolved: The courseware annexure (printed pp. 364-401) is the Indian Basel III capital annexure of earlier vintage. Differences found and resolved in favour of the 2025 Directions: the AFS reserve in CET1 and the quarterly profit conditions (audited or limited review), the add-on factors for market-related contracts (substituted from 10 March 2026), the list of rating agencies (seven, with SMERA now Acuite), unrated risk weight (150 per cent above ₹200 crore) and the securitisation haircut cell (24 against the courseware's 13). Later amendments to these Directions (notably after the 30 June 2026 cut-off, such as the fifth amendment of 8 May 2026) were not separated from the text read.

The courseware's list of risk weights by exposure type (residential and commercial real estate, capital market exposure, NBFCs, regulatory retail, staff loans and others) is of earlier vintage and is not taught; the Directions' risk weights for those classes were not tested in this batch. The guarantor risk weights (20 per cent for AAA, 30 per cent for AA) are the courseware's account.

The courseware glossary and remaining enclosures (printed pp. 389-401: operational requirements for collateral, netting and guarantees, the maturity factor table and glossary) were read only in part; the operational requirements for collateral and the glossary are not tested.

The Directions' deductions in detail (thresholds for significant investments in financial entities, treatment of the shortfall of provisions, and the transitional arrangements) were not recomputed; the deductions are taught as a list, not as thresholds, except the 10 per cent deferred tax asset recognition limit.
Reviewer for this batch is the authoring agent; no independent or human review.
